oneLineAnswer: A short-acting prescription sedative given by a clinician before procedures, and a nasal spray for seizure clusters.
whatItIs: Midazolam belongs to the benzodiazepine family. These medicines depress the central nervous system, which means they slow brain activity and cause sleepiness. Midazolam acts quickly and wears off quickly. Midazolam comes as an injection, as a nasal spray, and as an oral liquid. The nasal spray is sold under the brand name Nayzilam. Midazolam has been approved for use in the United States since 1985. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance, a category for drugs with a potential for abuse. Its chemical formula is C18H13ClFN3.
whatItDoes: Midazolam makes you drowsy and calm. It can also make you forget what happened.
It is given before or during procedures, and sometimes to keep patients comfortable on breathing machines.
Sedation begins within about 3 to 5 minutes when the medicine is injected into a vein.
In one label study, many patients could not recall pictures shown 30 minutes after an injection into a muscle.
The nasal spray is used to stop clusters of seizures in people with epilepsy.
howPeopleUseIt: A doctor or nurse gives midazolam. It is not a medicine you take on your own.
Labels say the injection should be used only where breathing and heart function are monitored continuously.
A caregiver can be trained to give the nasal spray when a seizure cluster starts.
An oral liquid form has been studied in children before surgery.
Labels recommend having a reversal medicine called flumazenil ready when the injection is used.

commonSideEffects: Breathing changes were the most frequent findings in label data.
Breathing depth or rate dropped in about 23 in 100 people after an injection into a vein.
After an injection into a muscle it dropped in about 11 in 100.
In children, low oxygen levels were recorded in about 5 in 100.
Brief breathing pauses and low blood pressure each occurred in about 3 in 100.
Some people had pain, hardness, redness or muscle stiffness where the injection went in.
Headache was reported in about 1 in 100 people after a muscle injection.
Rarely the opposite of calming happens. This is called a paradoxical reaction. It can look like agitation, irritability or confusion.
seriousSigns: The main danger is serious breathing depression, where breathing becomes slow, shallow or stops.
These events are reported most often when other brain-slowing medicines are given at the same time.
Mixing a benzodiazepine with an opioid pain medicine can cause deep sedation, breathing failure, coma and death.
A severe overdose can cause breathing failure and coma.
Stopping the medicine suddenly after heavy or long use can cause withdrawal.
The worst withdrawal symptoms have followed excessive doses over a long period.
whoShouldAvoid: Anyone with a known allergy to midazolam should not receive it.
People with acute narrow-angle glaucoma, a sudden rise in pressure inside the eye, should not receive it.
The injection contains benzyl alcohol, so labels rule it out for premature infants.
Labels say older adults aged 60 and over, and frail or debilitated people, need lower doses.
Labels say the injection must not be given as a rapid injection to newborns.

interactions: Opioid pain medicines are the most serious combination, because together they can cause profound sedation and stop breathing.
Benzodiazepines act at GABA A sites in the brain. Opioids act mainly at mu receptors, so the breathing effects add up.
Alcohol and any other medicine that slows the brain makes the sedative effect stronger.
A liver enzyme called CYP3A4 breaks midazolam down. Drugs that block this enzyme can raise its level in your body.
The label names cimetidine, erythromycin, diltiazem, verapamil, ketoconazole and itraconazole as medicines to be cautious with.
pregnancyAndChildren: Studies of pregnant women exposed to benzodiazepines have not shown a clear link to major birth defects. Those studies are observational, so they cannot prove the drug is safe or measure a small risk. Midazolam crosses the placenta, the organ that links a baby to its mother. It can cause breathing problems, floppy muscle tone and sedation in newborns. Labels advise watching exposed newborns for sedation and withdrawal. Midazolam passes into breast milk at low levels. One label says a breastfeeding woman may consider discarding milk for at least 4 to 8 hours. There is no data on whether midazolam affects milk production. In children, sedation use has been established in pediatric and neonatal patients. The nasal spray is approved for people with epilepsy aged 12 years and older.
whatWeDoNotKnow: The pregnancy data are observational, so they cannot rule out a small increase in birth defect risk.
Labels ask clinicians to assess the risk of abuse and addiction. They give no frequency for how often it happens.
Animal studies raise questions about brain development in young animals. The label says the human meaning is not clear.
There is no data on how midazolam affects milk production.
Most safety numbers in the label come from monitored medical settings, so they may not describe use elsewhere.
